1.1: The brothers, the Yahuḏim that are at Yerushalayim and in the land of Yahuḏah desire health and peace to the brothers, the Yahuḏim that are throughout Mitsrayim.
1.2: Elohim show favor to you, and remember His Covenant that He made with Aḇraham, Yitsḥaq, and Ya’aqoḇ His trustworthy servants;
1.3: and give you all a heart to serve Him and to do His desire with good courage and an eager mind.
1.4: And open your hearts in His Torah and Commands, and send you peace,
1.5: and hear your prayers, and be at one with you, and never forsake you in time of trouble.
1.6: And now we are here praying for you.
1.7: Such time as Dĕmĕtrios reigned, in the hundred and sixty-ninth year, we the Yahuḏim wrote to you in the extreme trouble that came upon us in those years, from the time that Yason and his company revolted from the qodesh land and reign,
1.8: and burned the porch and shed innocent blood; we then prayed to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and were heard. We also offered slaughterings and fine flour, and lit the lamps, and put out the loaves.
1.9: And now, see that you guard the Feast of Sukkoth in the month Kislĕw.
1.10: In the hundred and eighty-eighth year, the people that were at Yerushalayim and in Yahuḏah, and the council, and Yahuḏah, sent greeting and health to Aristobulos, Meleḵ Ptolemaeus’ master, who was of the descendants of the anointed kohenim, and to the Yahuḏim that were in Mitsrayim.
1.11: In so far as Elohim has delivered us from great perils, we thank Him highly, as having been in battle against a meleḵ.
1.12: For He threw out those that fought within the qodesh city.
1.13: For when the leader had come to Paras, and the army with him that seemed invincible, they were slain in the temple of Nanaia by deceit of the priests of Nanaia.
1.14: For Antioḵos and his friends that were with him came into the place as though he would marry her, to receive silver in name of a dowry.
1.15: Which when the priests of Nanaia had presented and he had entered into the surrounds of the temple with a small company, they shut the temple as soon as Antioḵos had come in.
1.16: And opening a secret door of the roof, they threw stones like thunderbolts, and struck down the captain, cut them in pieces, smote off their heads and threw them to those that were outside.
1.17: Baruḵ be our Elohim in all, who has delivered up the wicked.
1.18: Therefore now that we have purposed to guard the purification of the Hĕyḵal on the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislĕw, we thought it necessary to notify you of this, that you also might guard it, as the Feast of the Sukkoth, and of the fire which was given to us when Neḥemyah brought an offering after he had built the Hĕyḵal and the altar.
1.19: For when our fathers were led into Paras, the kohenim that were then dedicated took the fire of the altar secretly, and hid it in a hollow place of a well without water, where they kept it safe, so that the place was unknown to all men.
1.20: Now after many years, when it pleased Elohim, Neḥemyah, having been sent from the meleḵ of Paras, sent the descendants of those kohenim that had hid the fire. But when they told us they found no fire, but thick water;
1.21: he then commanded them to draw it up, and to bring it. And when the slaughterings were laid, Neḥemyah commanded the kohenim to sprinkle the wood and the matters laid upon it with the water.
1.22: When this was done, and the time came that the sun shone, which was hid in the cloud before, there was a great fire kindled, so that every man marveled.
1.23: And the kohenim made a prayer while the slaughtering was consumed; both the kohenim and all the rest - Yahonathan beginning, and the rest answering to it - as Neḥemyah did.
1.24: And the prayer was after this manner: “O 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, Aḏonai, Elohim, Creator of all things who is awesome and mighty and righteous and showing favor and the only kind Meleḵ,
1.25: the only Giver of all things, the only righteous, almighty and everlasting. You who delivers Yisra’ĕl from all trouble and chose the fathers and qadosh them.
1.26: “Receive the offering for all Your people Yisra’ĕl and preserve Your own portion and qadosh them.
1.27: “Gather together those that are scattered from us, deliver those that serve among the gentiles, look upon those who are despised and abhorred and let the gentiles know that You are our Elohim.
1.28: “Punish those that oppress us and do evil to us with pride.
1.29: “Plant Your people again in Your qodesh place as Mosheh has spoken.”
1.30: And the kohenim sang songs of thanksgiving.
1.31: Now when the offering was consumed, Neḥemyah commanded the water that was left to be poured on the great stones.
1.32: When this was done, there was a flame kindled, and it was added to by the light that shone from the altar.
1.33: So when this matter was known, it was told the meleḵ of Paras, that in the place where the kohenim that were led away had hid the fire, there appeared water, and that Neḥemyah had purified the offerings with it.
1.34: Then the meleḵ, enclosing the place, qadosh it, after he had examined the matter.
1.35: And the meleḵ took many gifts, and bestowed them on those whom he would esteem.
1.36: And Neḥemyah called this Naphthar, which is to say, a cleansing; but many men call it Nephtar.

10.1: Now with 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 guiding them Maqqaḇah and his army recovered the Hĕyḵal and the city.
10.2: And they pulled down the altars and also the chapels which the gentiles had built in the open street.
10.3: And having cleansed the Hĕyḵal they made another altar, and striking flint they made fire out of it and offered a slaughtering after two years, and offered incense and lamps and showbread.
10.4: When that was done, they bowed down and pleaded to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 that they would no longer come upon such troubles; but if they sinned any more against Him, that He Himself would discipline them with kindness, and that they would not be delivered over to the blasphemous and foreign nations.
10.5: Now on the same day that the foreigners profaned the Hĕyḵal; on that very same day it was cleansed again, even the twenty-fifth day of the same month, which is Kislĕw.
10.6: And they observed the eight days with gladness, as in the Feast of Sukkoth, remembering that not long before they had held the Feast of Sukkoth, as when they wandered in the mountains and caves like beasts.
10.7: Therefore they carried branches and leafy twigs and also palms, and sang tehillim to He that had given them good success in cleansing His Place.
10.8: They also made a law by common decree, that every year those days should be observed by the whole nation of the Yahuḏim.
10.9: And this was the end of Antioḵos, called Epiphanĕs.
10.10: Now we shall declare the acts of Antioḵos Eupator, who was the son of this wicked man, assembling briefly the calamities of the battles.
10.11: So when he had attained the crown, he appointed a certain Lusias over the affairs of his reign, and appointed him his chief governor of Koĕlĕ Suria and Phoinikĕ.
10.12: For Ptolemaeus, who was called Makron, choosing rather to do righteousness to the Yahuḏim for the wrong that had been done to them, sought to continue peace with them.
10.13: So being accused by the meleḵ’s friends before Eupator, and called a traitor at every command that Philometor had given to him, because he had left Kupros and departed to Antioḵos Epiphanĕs. And seeing that he was in a dishonorable position, he was so discouraged that he poisoned himself and died.
10.14: But when Gorgias was governor of the towers, he hired soldiers and maintained battle continually with the Yahuḏim.
10.15: And also the Eḏomites, having taken into their hands the most advantageous towers, kept the Yahuḏim occupied and accepting those that were banished from Yerushalayim, they prepared to engage in battle.
10.16: Then those that were with Maqqaḇah pleaded and sought Elohim that He would be their Helper; and so they ran with force upon the strongholds of the Eḏomites.
10.17: And attacking them mightily, they gained the towers and held off all that fought on the wall and slew all that fell into their hands, and killed no fewer than twenty thousand.
10.18: And because some, who were no less than nine thousand, had fled together into two very strong fortresses, having all the provisions necessary to sustain the siege,
10.19: Maqqaḇah left Shim’on and Yosĕph and also Zakkai and those that were with him, who were enough to besiege them, and he departed to those places which needed his help more.
10.20: Now those that were with Shim’on, being led by covetousness, were persuaded with silver by some of those that were in the fortress, and took seventy thousand draḵmas and let some of them escape.
10.21: But when Maqqaḇah was told what was done, he called the governors of the people together and accused those men, that they had sold their brothers for silver and released their enemies to fight against them.
10.22: So he slew those that were found traitors and immediately took the two fortresses.
10.23: And having good skill with all weapons he took in hand, he slew more than twenty thousand in the two towers.
10.24: Now when Timotheos, whom the Yahuḏim had overcome before, had gathered a great multitude of foreign armies, and not a few horses from Asia, came intending to take the Yahuḏim by force.
10.25: But when he drew near, those that were with Maqqaḇah turned to pray to Elohim, and threw dust on their heads and girded their loins with sackcloth,
10.26: and fell down at the foot of the altar and pleaded for Him to be kind to them and to be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the Torah declares.
10.27: So after the prayer they took their weapons and went further on from the city; and when they drew near to their enemies, they remained secluded.
10.28: Now early when the sun had risen, they both engaged in battle; the one group having their strength together with also their refuge in 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 for a promise of their win and deliverance, the other side making rage the leader of their battle.
10.29: But when the battle grew fierce, five radiant men from the shamayim on horses appeared to the enemy, with bridles of gold. And two of them led the Yahuḏim,
10.30: and took Maqqaḇah between them, and covered him on every side with weapons, guarding him and shooting arrows and lightning against the enemy, so that being confused with blindness and troubled, they were killed.
10.31: And there were twenty thousand five hundred footmen slain, and six hundred horsemen.
10.32: As for Timotheos himself, he fled into a stronghold, called Gezer, where Ḵaereas was governor.
10.33: But those that were with Maqqaḇah laid siege against the fortress courageously for four days.
10.34: And those that were within, trusting in the strength of the place, blasphemed exceedingly, and spoke wicked words.
10.35: Nevertheless, early on the fifth day, twenty young men of Maqqaḇah’s army filled with wrath because of the blasphemies, assaulted the wall bravely and with great courage killed all those they encountered.
10.36: Others also going up after them, while they were occupied with those that were within, burned the towers, and lighting fires burned the blasphemers alive. And others broke open the gates, and having let in the rest of the army, took the city
10.37: and killed Timotheos who was hiding in some pit, with Ḵaereas his brother and Apollophanĕs.
10.38: When this was done, they baraḵ 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 with tehillim and thanksgiving who had done such greatness for Yisra’ĕl, and given them the victory.

11.1: Not long after, Lusias the meleḵ’s protector and cousin, who also managed the affairs, took great displeasure in that which was done.
11.2: And when he had gathered about eighty thousand with all the horsemen, he came against the Yahuḏim, thinking to make the city a dwelling for the gentiles,
11.3: and to make a profit from the Hĕyḵal, as from the other temples of the gentiles, and to put up the high kehunnah for sale every year;
11.4: not at all considering the power of Elohim, but puffed up with his tens of thousands of footmen, and his thousands of horsemen, and his eighty elephants.
11.5: So he came to Yahuḏah, and drew near to Bĕyth Tsur which was a fortified town, but about five stadion away from Yerushalayim, and he laid heavy siege to it.
11.6: Now when those that were with Maqqaḇah heard that he besieged the towers, they and all the people pleaded to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 with lamentation and tears that He would send a good messenger to deliver Yisra’ĕl.
11.7: Then Maqqaḇah himself took weapons first of all, encouraging the others to risk their lives together with him to help their brothers. So they went out together with one mind.
11.8: And while they were at Yerushalayim, there appeared before them one in white garments on horseback, brandishing his weapons of gold.
11.9: Then they baraḵ the kind Elohim all together and took courage, so that they were ready not only to fight with men, but with most fierce beasts, and to break through walls of iron.
11.10: So they marched forward with their weapons, having a Helper from the shamayim, for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 was kind to them.
11.11: And making a charge on their enemies like lions, they slew eleven thousand footmen and sixteen hundred horsemen, and put all the others to flight.
11.12: Also many of them escaped stripped and wounded, and Lusias himself fled away shamefully and escaped.
11.13: Being a man of understanding, accepting the loss he had, and considering that the Iḇrim could not be overcome because Ĕl Shaddai helped them, he sent to them
11.14: and persuaded them to agree to all reasonable conditions, and promised that he would persuade the meleḵ that he must be a friend to them.
11.15: Then Maqqaḇah consented to all that Lusias desired, being careful of the common good, and whatever Maqqaḇah wrote to Lusias concerning the Yahuḏim, the meleḵ granted it.
11.16: For there were letters written to the Yahuḏim from Lusias to this effect: “Lusias to the people of the Yahuḏim, greetings.
11.17: “Yoḥanan and Aḇshalom, who were sent from you, delivered the written request and asked for the completion of it’s contents.
11.18: “Therefore whatever matters were right to be reported to the meleḵ, I have declared them, and he has granted as much as possible.
11.19: “And if you will then keep yourselves loyal to the state, from now on I will also endeavor to be a source for your good.
11.20: “And of these matters I have given order both to these and the others that came from me, to speak with you.
11.21: “Farewell. The hundred and forty-eighth year, the twenty-fourth day of the month Dioskorinthios.”
11.22: Now the meleḵ’s letter contained these words: “Meleḵ Antioḵos to his brother Lusias sends greeting.
11.23: “Since our father is taken up to the mighty ones, our desire is, that those that are in our reign live peaceably, that everyone may attend to his own affairs.
11.24: “We also understand that the Yahuḏim would not agree with our father to be brought into the custom of the gentiles, but rather keep their own manner of living; which is the reason they ask from us that we should allow them to live after their own laws.
11.25: “Therefore our decision is, that this nation shall be at peace and we have determined to restore them their Hĕyḵal that they may live according to the customs of their forefathers.
11.26: “You shall do well therefore to send to them and grant them peace, that when they are informed of our decision, they may take courage and always go cheerfully about their own affairs.”
11.27: And the letter of the meleḵ to the nation of the Yahuḏim was in this manner: “Meleḵ Antioḵos sends greeting to the council, and the rest of the Yahuḏim.
11.28: “If you are well, we have our desire; we are also in good health.
11.29: “Menelaos has informed us, that your desire was to return home and to follow your own business,
11.30: therefore those that would depart shall have safe conduct with safety till the thirtieth day of Xanthikos.
11.31: “And the Yahuḏim shall apply their own kind of food and Laws as before; and none of them in any way shall be provoked for whatever is done in ignorance.
11.32: “I have sent also Menelaos, that he may encourage you.
11.33: “Farewell. In the hundred forty and eighth year, and the fifteenth day of the month Xanthikos.”
11.34: The Romans also sent a letter to them containing these words: “Quintus Memmius and Titus Manlius, ambassadors of the Romans, sends greeting to the people of the Yahuḏim.
11.35: “Whatever Lusias the meleḵ’s cousin has granted, with that we are also well pleased.
11.36: “But regarding such matters that he has decided to be referred to the meleḵ, after you have advised of this, send someone promptly that we may declare as it is appropriate for you, for we are now going to Antioḵeia.
11.37: “Therefore send messengers with speed, so that we may know what is your decision.
11.38: “Farewell. This hundred and forty-eighth year, the fifteenth day of the month Xanthikos.”

12.1: When these covenants were made, Lusias went to the meleḵ, and the Yahuḏim were within their land.
12.2: But of the governors of several places, Timotheos and Apollonios the son of Genneus, also Hieronumos and Dĕmophon, and besides them, Nikanor the governor of Kupros, would not allow them to be at rest and live in peace.
12.3: The men of Yapho also did a very wicked deed: they asked the Yahuḏim that dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into the boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no harm.
12.4: Who accepted according to the common decree of the city, desiring to live in peace and suspecting naught. But when they had gone out into the deep, they drowned no less than two hundred of them.
12.5: When Yahuḏah heard of this cruelty done to his countrymen, he commanded those that were with him to ready themselves.
12.6: And calling upon Elohim the righteous Judge, he came against those murderers of his brothers, and burned the harbor by night, and lit the boats on fire, and he slew those that attempted to flee.
12.7: And when the town was shut up, he withdrew, intending to return to root out all those of the city of Yapho.
12.8: But when he heard that the Yaḇne’ĕlites were planning to do the same to the Yahuḏim that dwelt among them,
12.9: he came upon the Yaḇne’ĕlites again by night, and lit the harbor on fire and the fleet, so that the light of the fire was seen at Yerushalayim two hundred and forty stadion away.
12.10: Now when they had gone nine stadion from there on their march against Timotheos, no less than five thousand footmen and five hundred Araḇian horsemen attacked him.
12.11: So there was a very fierce battle, but with the help of Elohim Yahuḏah’s side overcame. So the Nomads of Araḇia, having been overcome, begged Yahuḏah for peace, promising to give him both cattle and to fulfill other delights.
12.12: Then Yahuḏah, thinking that they would indeed be profitable in many ways, granted them peace. Therefore they shook hands, and so they departed to their tents.
12.13: He also constructed a bridge to a certain strong city, which was fortified around about with walls, and inhabited by people of various nations; and the name of it was Kasphor.
12.14: But those that were within put such trust in the strength of the walls and stores of food, that they behaved rudely toward those that were with Yahuḏah, cursing and blaspheming and speaking such words which should not be spoken.
12.15: Therefore Yahuḏah and his army - calling on 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty of the world, who without rams or siege engines threw down Yeriḥo in the time of Yahoshua - gave a fierce assault against the walls,
12.16: and took the city by the desire of Elohim, and slew innumerable numbers so that an adjoining lake near there two stadion across, being full, was seen running with blood.
12.17: Then they moved on seven hundred and fifty stadion from there, and came to Ḵaraka to the Yahuḏim that are called Toḇians.
12.18: But as for Timotheos, they did not find him in the area, for before he had done any matter, he departed from there, having left a very strong garrison in a certain tower.
12.19: However Dositheos and Sosipatros, who were Maqqaḇah’s captains went out and slew those that Timotheos had left in the fortress - over ten thousand men.
12.20: And Maqqaḇah arranged his army in divisions and appointed them over the divisions, and went against Timotheos, who had a hundred and twenty thousand footmen and two thousand five hundred horsemen with him.
12.21: Now when Timotheos knew of Yahuḏah’s approach, he sent the women and children and the extra baggage to a fortress called Qarnayim, because the town was hard to besiege, and difficult to assault because of the steepness of all the approaches.
12.22: But when Yahuḏah’s first division came into sight, the enemies fled, being smitten with fear and terror with the appearance of He who sees all things; one running this way, another that way, so that many of them were injured by their own men, and wounded with the points of their own swords.
12.23: Yahuḏah was also very earnest in pursuit of them, killing those wicked wretches, of whom he slew about thirty thousand men.
12.24: And Timotheos himself fell into the hands of Dositheos and Sosipatros, whom he begged with much guile to let him go with his life, because he had many of the Yahuḏim’s parents and the brothers of some of them, who if they put him to death, would be shown no regard.
12.25: So when he had assured them with many words that he would restore them without harm, they let him go according to the agreement for the deliverance of their brothers.
12.26: Then Maqqaḇah marched onward to Qarnayim and to the temple of Atarathĕh, and he slow twenty-five thousand people there.
12.27: And after he had put them to flight and destroyed them, Yahuḏah moved the army toward Ephron, a strong city in which Lusias dwelt, and a great multitude of various nations. And the strong young men guarded the walls, and also defended them mightily with a great supply of weapons and arrows inside.
12.28: But when Yahuḏah and his army had called upon Ĕl Shaddai, who with His power breaks the strength of His enemies, they took the city and slew twenty and five thousand of those that were in it.
12.29: From there they departed to Bĕyth She’an, which lies six hundred stadion from Yerushalayim.
12.30: But when the Yahuḏim that dwelt there had witnessed that the Skuthopolitans were friendly to them, and treated them kindly in the time of their adversity,
12.31: they thanked them, desiring them to continue being friendly toward them. And so they came to Yerushalayim - the Festival of Shaḇuoth approaching.
12.32: And after the Festival called Shaḇuoth, they went out against Gorgias the governor of Eḏom,
12.33: who came out with three thousand footmen and four hundred horsemen.
12.34: And it came to be that a few of the Yahuḏim were slain in the battle,
12.35: at which time Dositheos, one of Bakenor’s division who was a strong man and on horseback, was still upon Gorgias. And taking hold of his cloak dragged him with force. But when he would have taken that cursed man alive, a horseman of Thrakeia coming upon him cut off his arm, allowing Gorgias to flee to Marisa.
12.36: Now when those that were with Gorgias had fought long and were weary. Yahuḏah called upon 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 that He would show Himself to be their Helper and Leader of the battle.
12.37: And with that, he began and sung tehillim with a loud voice in his own language, and charging on Gorgias’ men unaware, he put them to flight.
12.38: So Yahuḏah gathered his army, and came into the city of Aḏullam, and when the seventh day came, they purified themselves, as was the custom, and kept the Shabbath in that very place.
12.39: And on the following day, as the practice had been, Yahuḏah and his army came to take up the bodies of them that were slain, and to bury them with their relatives in their fathers’ graves.
12.40: Now under the cloaks of every one that was slain they found objects dedicated to the idols of Yaḇneh, which are forbidden by the Torah for the Yahuḏim. Then every man saw that this was the reason why they had been slain.
12.41: All men therefore baraḵ 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the righteous Judge, who had revealed that which was hidden,
12.42: committed themselves to prayer, and begged Him that the sin committed might be completely blotted out of remembrance. Righteous Yahuḏah also encouraged the people to keep themselves from sin, because they saw before their eyes that which came upon those that were slain for their sins.
12.43: And when he had gathered from throughout the army the sum of two thousand draḵmas of silver, he sent it to Yerushalayim to offer a sin offering, acting very well and honorable in doing so, bearing in mind the resurrection.
12.44: For if he had not had expectancy that those that were slain would rise again, it would be unnecessary and worthless to pray for the dead.
12.45: And he also perceived that there was great favor stored up for those who died righteously, which was a qodesh and good thought. So he made an atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from sin.

13.1: In the hundred and forty-ninth year Yahuḏah was informed Antioḵos Eupator was approaching Yahuḏah with a great force
13.2: with Lusias his guardian and governor with him, each having a Yawanite force of a hundred and ten thousand footmen and five thousand three hundred horsemen and twenty-two elephants and three hundred chariots armed with scythes.
13.3: Menelaos also joined himself with them and encouraged Antioḵos with great deception; not for the safeguard of the country, but because he thought he may have been made governor.
13.4: But the Meleḵ of melaḵim moved Antioḵos against the wicked wretch, and Lusias informed the meleḵ that this man was the reason for all the evil, so that the meleḵ commanded to bring him to Beroia, and to put him to death by the method of the place.
13.5: Now there was a tower of fifty ammah high in that place full of ashes, and it had a round turret on which every side hung down into the ashes.
13.6: And whoever was condemned of temple robbery or had committed any other grievous crime, there all men were thrown to their death.
13.7: And quite righteously such a death to die came upon that wicked man, not having so much as burial in the earth.
13.8: Because he had committed many sins pertaining to the altar, whose fire and ashes were qodesh, so he received his death in ashes.
13.9: Now the meleḵ came with a wicked and haughty plan to do far worse to the Yahuḏim than had been done in his father’s time.
13.10: When Yahuḏah learned of this, he commanded the multitude to call on 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 night and day that He would help them now if ever at any other time, being at the point of being removed their Torah, from their country and from the qodesh Hĕyḵal;
13.11: and that He would not allow the people that had only just now been a little refreshed, to be in subjection to the blasphemous nations.
13.12: So when they had all done this together and pleaded for the kindness of Elohim with weeping and fasting and lying flat upon the ground for three days, Yahuḏah, having encouraged them, commanded they should make themselves ready.
13.13: And Yahuḏah, determined privately with the elders, that before the meleḵ’s army could enter Yahuḏah, and take the city, to go out and determine the matter in battle with the help of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
13.14: So when he had committed all to the Creator of the world and encouraged his soldiers to fight bravely, even to death, for the Laws, the Hĕyḵal, the city, the country and the citizenship, he encamped by Modi’im.
13.15: And having given the watchword to those that were with him, “Victory is of Elohim,” he went into the meleḵ’s camp by night with the bravest and chosen young men and slew about four thousand men in the camp, and the leading elephant with all that were upon it.
13.16: And by the end they had filled the camp with fear and disorder and withdrew with good success.
13.17: This was done at daybreak because the protection of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 helped him.
13.18: Now when the meleḵ had a taste of the courage of the Yahuḏim, he attempted to take the towers using strategy,
13.19: and marched toward Bĕyth Tsur, which was a stronghold of the Yahuḏim; but he failed, was put to flight and lost his men,
13.20: for Yahuḏah had dispatched to those that were in it that which was necessary.
13.21: But Rhodokos, who was in the Yahuḏim’s army, disclosed secrets to the enemies; therefore he was sought out, and when they had taken him, they put him in prison.
13.22: The meleḵ made a treaty with those in Bĕyth Tsur a second time, gave his pledge, took theirs, departed, fought with Yahuḏah, was overcome;
13.23: heard that Philippos, who was left over the affairs in Antioḵeia was hard pressed, being confounded made a treaty with the Yahuḏim, submitted himself and swore to all equal conditions, agreed with them and brought an offering, honored the Hĕyḵal and dealt kindly with the place.
13.24: And accepting good from Maqqaḇah, made him principal governor from Ptolemais to the Gerarians,
13.25: and went to Ptolemais. The people there were grieved because of the covenants, and they raged for they wanted to annul their covenants.
13.26: Lusias went up to the judgment seat, said as much as he could in defense of the cause, persuaded, pacified, appeased them and returned to Antioḵeia. So it was regarding the meleḵ’s coming and going.

14.1: After three years Yahuḏah was informed that Dĕmĕtrios the son of Seleukus, having entered by the harbor of Tripolis with a fleet of great strength,
14.2: had taken the country and killed Antioḵos, and Lusias his guardian.
14.3: Now a certain Elyaqim, who had been kohĕn ha’gadol, and had deliberately defiled himself in the times of their mixing with the gentiles, seeing he could not save himself by any means, nor have any more access to the qodesh altar,
14.4: came to Meleḵ Dĕmĕtrios in the hundred and fifty-first year, presenting a crown of gold to him and a palm, and also the branches which were used on Festivals in the Hĕyḵal. But that day he remained silent.
14.5: However having taken opportunity to further his foolish plan, and being called into counsel by Dĕmĕtrios and asked how the Yahuḏim stood affected and what they intended, he answered in this way:
14.6: “Those of the Yahuḏim that are called Ḥasiḏim, whose captain is Yahuḏah Maqqaḇah, fight continually and are treasonous and will not let the others be at peace.
14.7: “I therefore, being deprived of the honor of my ancestors, meaning the high kehunnah, have now come here.
14.8: “First indeed for the sincere concern I have of matters pertaining to the meleḵ, and secondly, even after that, I intend for the good of my own countrymen; for all our nation is in no small grief through the foolishness of those already mentioned.
14.9: “Therefore O meleḵ, seeing you know all these matters, have concern for this country and our nation which is pressed on every side, according to the gentleness that you readily show to all.
14.10: “For as long as Yahuḏah lives, it is not possible for the nation to be at rest.”
14.11: No sooner was this said of him, when other friends of the meleḵ, being wickedly disposed toward Yahuḏah, enraged Dĕmĕtrios further.
14.12: And promptly calling Nikanor, who had been chief over the elephants, and making him governor over Yahuḏah, he sent him out,
14.13: commanding him to slay Yahuḏah and to scatter those that were with him, and to make Elyaqim kohĕn ha’gadol of the great Hĕyḵal.
14.14: Then the gentiles that had fled out from Yahuḏah out of Yahuḏah, flocked to Nikanor, thinking the harm and destruction of the Yahuḏim to be to their advantage.
14.15: Now when the Yahuḏim heard of Nikanor’s coming, and that the gentiles were against them, they threw dust on their heads and pleaded to He who had established His people forever, and who always helps His portion with manifestation of His presence.
14.16: So at the command of the captain they immediately moved from there and approached those at the town of Dessaou.
14.17: Now Shim’on, Yahuḏah’s brother, had joined in battle with Nikanor, but was somewhat confused through the sudden silence of his enemies.
14.18: Nevertheless Nikanor, hearing of the courage of those that were with Yahuḏah, and the courage that they had to fight for their country, did not dare try the matter by the sword.
14.19: Therefore he sent Poseidonius and Theodotus and Mattithyahu to make peace.
14.20: So when they had spent a long time taking counsel and the captain had made the multitude aware of this and it appeared that they were all of one mind, they agreed to the covenants,
14.21: and appointed a day to meet together by themselves. And when the day came, and chairs were placed for either of them,
14.22: Yahuḏah positioned soldiers at the ready in suitable places, lest some treachery should suddenly be taken by the enemies; so they held peace negotiations.
14.23: Now Nikanor dwelt in Yerushalayim, and did no harm, but sent away the people that came flocking to him.
14.24: And he would not readily allow Yahuḏah out of his sight, for he loved the man from his heart.
14.25: He asked him to also take a wife, and to bring forth children; so he married, was peaceable, and shared in this life.
14.26: But Elyaqim, perceiving the love that was between them, and considering the covenants that were made, came to Dĕmĕtrios and told him that Nikanor was disloyal to the government, in that he had ordained Yahuḏah, a traitor to his reign, to be successor to the meleḵ.
14.27: Then the meleḵ being enraged and provoked with the accusations of this very wicked man, wrote to Nikanor signifying that he was very displeased with the covenants, and commanded that he send Maqqaḇah prisoner in all haste to Antioḵeia.
14.28: When this came to Nikanor’s hearing, he was very troubled within himself, and was grieved that he should annul the conditions that were agreed upon, the man having done no wrong.
14.29: But because there was no going against the meleḵ, he watched for his time to accomplish this matter strategically.
14.30: However, when Maqqaḇah saw that Nikanor began to harden toward him, and that he dealt with him more roughly than he used to, perceiving that such sour behavior did not come from goodness, he gathered not a few of his men together, and withdrew himself from Nikanor.
14.31: But the other, knowing that he was obviously hindered by Yahuḏah’s strategy, came into the great and qadosh Hĕyḵal, and commanded the kohenim that were offering their usual slaughterings to deliver the man to him.
14.32: And when they swore that they could not tell where the man whom he sought was,
14.33: he stretched out his right hand toward the Hĕyḵal, and made this oath: “If you will not deliver me Yahuḏah as a prisoner, I will lay this Hĕyḵal of Elohim even to the ground, and I will break down the altar, and build a splendid temple to Dionusos!”
14.34: After these words he departed. Then the kohenim lifted up their hands toward the shamayim, and pleaded to Him who was always a defender of their nation, saying,
14.35: “You, O Aḏon of all, who has need of nothing, was pleased that the Hĕyḵal of Your dwelling should be among us.
14.36: “Now therefore, O qodesh Aḏon of all qodeshah, keep this House which was recently cleansed, undefiled forever, and stop every unrighteous mouth.”
14.37: Now a certain Razis, one of the elders of Yerushalayim, a lover of his countrymen and a man of very good report, who for his kindness was called a father of the Yahuḏim, was accused before Nikanor.
14.38: For formerly, when they had not mixed themselves with the gentiles, he had been accused of Yahuḏaism, and boldly risked his body and life with all vehemency for the belief of the Yahuḏim.
14.39: So Nikanor, wanting to show the hate that he held for the Yahuḏim, sent over five hundred men of battle to capture him.
14.40: For he thought to do the Yahuḏim much harm by taking him.
14.41: Now when the multitude had almost taken the tower and violently broken through the outer door and called for fire to be brought to burn it, he, being ready to be taken on every side fell upon his sword;
14.42: choosing to die bravely rather than to fall into the hands of the wicked, to be abused otherwise appropriate to his noble birth.
14.43: But missing his stroke through haste, the multitude also rushing within the doors, he ran boldly up to the wall and threw himself down bravely among the thickest of them.
14.44: But when they quickly retreated, and made a space, he fell down into the midst of the empty space.
14.45: Nevertheless, while there was still breath within him, being inflamed with wrath, he rose up; and though his blood gushed out like spouts of water, and his wounds were severe, he ran through the midst of the crowd. And standing upon a steep rock,
14.46: when his blood was now almost gone, he gathered out his bowels, and taking them in both his hands, he threw them upon the crowd. And calling upon the Aḏon of Ḥai and Ruaḥ to restore those again; therefore he died.

15.1: But Nikanor, hearing that Yahuḏah and his army were in the strongholds around Shomeron, resolved to attack them without any defense on the Shabbath day.
15.2: Nevertheless the Yahuḏim that were compelled to go with him said, “Do not destroy so cruelly and ruthlessly, but give honor to that day, which He who sees all things has honored with qodeshah above all other days.”
15.3: Then that most shameful wretch demanded, if there were a Mighty One in the shamayim, that had commanded the Shabbath day to be guarded!
15.4: And when they said, “There is in the shamayim a living Aḏon, and Ĕl, who commanded the seventh day to be guarded.”
15.5: Then the other said, “And I also am mighty upon the earth, and I command to take arms, and to do the meleḵ’s work!” But he did not succeed in having his wicked plan done.
15.6: So with great pride and haughtiness Nikanor determined to put up a public monument of his victory over Yahuḏah and those that were with him.
15.7: But Maqqaḇah had assured confidence that 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 would help him,
15.8: therefore he encouraged his people not to fear the gentiles coming against them, but to remember the help which they had received from the shamayim in former times, and now to expect the deliverance and help, which would come to them from the Almighty.
15.9: And so encouraging them from the Torah and the neḇi’im, and reminding them of the battles that they had won before, he encouraged them further.
15.10: And when he had stirred up their spirits, he gave them their orders, also showing them the falsehood of the gentiles, and the breach of oaths.
15.11: So he armed every one of them, not so much with defense of shields and spears, as with encouragement and good words; and besides that, he told them a dream worthy of belief, as if it had indeed been so, which encouraged them not a little.
15.12: And this was his vision: That Onyah - a virtuous and a good man who had been kohĕn ha’gadol, reverent in conversation, gentle in spirit, also well spoken and taught in all points of righteousness from a young age - holding up his hands, prayed for the whole body of the Yahuḏim.
15.13: Having done this, there also appeared a man with grey hair, and exceedingly splendid, who was a wonder of excellence and majesty.
15.14: Then Onyah answered, saying, “This is a lover of the brothers who prays much for the people and for the qodesh city, that is, Yirmeyahu the naḇi of Elohim.”
15.15: So Yirmeyahu holding out his right hand gave Yahuḏah a sword of gold, and in giving it said,
15.16: “Take this qodesh sword - a gift from Elohim - with which you shall smite the adversaries.”
15.17: Thus being well encouraged by the words of Yahuḏah which were very good, and able to stir them up with bravery and to encourage the hearts of the young men, they determined not to pitch camp, but to courageously attack them, and to bravely try the matter in battle, because the city and the Miqdash and the Hĕyḵal were in danger.
15.18: For the concern that they had for their wives and their children, their brothers and families, was less for them; but the greatest and main fear was for the qodesh Hĕyḵal.
15.19: Those that were in the city were also not the least concerned, being troubled for the struggle abroad.
15.20: And now, when all looked what was to be the trial, and the enemies had already come near and the army was in battle array and the beasts strategically positioned and the horsemen positioned on the flanks,
15.21: Maqqaḇah seeing the approach of the multitude and the various preparations of armor and the ferocity of the beasts, stretched out his hands toward the shamayim, and called upon 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 who works wonders, knowing that deliverance does not come by weapons, but even as it seems good to Him, He gives to those who are worthy.
15.22: Therefore in his prayer he spoke in this way; “O 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, You sent Your messenger in the time of Yeḥizqiyahu meleḵ of Yahuḏah and slew five thousand eight hundred in the army of Sanḥĕriḇ.
15.23: “Therefore now also, O Aḏon of the shamayim, send a good messenger before us for a fear and dread upon them.
15.24: “And through the might of Your arm let those who come against Your qodesh people to blaspheme be stricken with terror.” And so he ended.
15.25: Then Nikanor and those that were with him came forward with trumpets and songs,
15.26: but Yahuḏah and his army countered the enemies with supplication and prayer,
15.27: so fighting with their hands and praying to Elohim with their hearts, they slew no less than thirty-five thousand men; for they were greatly encouraged through the manifestation of Elohim.
15.28: Now when the battle was over, returning again with joy, they knew that Nikanor lay dead in his armor.
15.29: Then they made a great shout and a noise, as they baraḵ the Almighty in their own language.
15.30: And Yahuḏah, who was ever the chief defender of the people both in body and mind, and who continued his love toward his countrymen all his life, commanded to strike off Nikanor’s head, and his arm at the shoulder, and bring them to Yerushalayim.
15.31: So when he was there and called those of his nation together and appointed the kohenim before the altar, he sent for those that were in the tower,
15.32: and showed them vile Nikanor’s head, and the arm of that blasphemer, which he had stretched out against the qodesh Hĕyḵal of the Almighty with proud boastings.
15.33: And when he had cut out the tongue of that wicked Nikanor, he commanded that they should give the pieces to the birds, and hang up the reward of his madness opposite the Hĕyḵal.
15.34: So every man baraḵ the esteemed Aḏon toward the shamayim saying, “Baruḵ be He that has kept His own Place undefiled!”
15.35: He also hung Nikanor’s head upon the tower, a clear and visible sign to all of the help of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
15.36: And they all appointed with a common decree to by no means let that day pass without honor, but to celebrate the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, which in the Surian tongue is called Aḏar, the day before Mordeḵai’s day.
15.37: So it came to be for Nikanor; and from that time on the Iḇrim had the city in their possession. And here I make an end.
15.38: And if I have done well, and as befits the story, it is that which I desired. But if scant and poorly, it is the best I could do.
15.39: For as it is harmful to drink wine or water alone, and as wine mingled with water is pleasant and delights the taste; even so, words finely formed delights the ears of those that read the story. And here shall be the end.

2.1: It is also found in the records that Yirmeyahu the naḇi commanded those that were carried away to take from the fire, as it has been declared,
2.2: and how the naḇi, having given them the Torah, charged them not to forget the Commands of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and that they should not stray in their minds when they see images of silver and gold with their ornaments.
2.3: And with other such words he urged them that the Torah should not depart from their hearts.
2.4: It was also contained in the same writing, that the naḇi, being warned by Elohim, commanded the Mishkan and the ark to go with him as he went up to the mountain where Mosheh climbed up and saw the inheritance of Elohim.
2.5: And when Yirmeyahu came there, he found a hollow cave where he laid the Mishkan and the ark and the altar of incense, and so sealed the entrance.
2.6: And some of those that followed him came to mark the way, but they could not find it.
2.7: When Yirmeyahu saw this, he charged them saying, “As for that place, it shall be unknown until the time that Elohim gathers his people together again and receives them in kindness.
2.8: “Then 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 shall show them these matters and the esteem of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 shall appear and also the cloud as it was shown under Mosheh, and as when Shelomoh desired that the place might be qadosh with honor.”
2.9: It was also declared, that he, being wise, offered the slaughtering of dedication and of the finishing of the Hĕyḵal.
2.10: And as when Mosheh prayed to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, the fire came down from the shamayim and consumed the offerings. Even as Shelomoh also prayed and the fire came down from the shamayim and consumed the burnt offerings.
2.11: And Mosheh said, “Because the sin offering was not to be eaten, it was consumed.”
2.12: So Shelomoh kept those eight days.
2.13: The same matters were also reported in the writings and commentaries of Neḥemyah; and how he, establishing a library, gathered together the acts of the melaḵim and the neḇi’im and of Dawiḏ and the letters of the melaḵim concerning the qodesh gifts.
2.14: Likewise, Yahuḏah also gathered together all those matters that were lost because of the battle we had, and they remain with us.
2.15: Therefore if you have need of these, send some to bring them to you.
2.16: Now that we are about to celebrate the purification, we have written to you, and you shall do well, if you guard the same days.
2.17: We also trust, that the Elohim who delivered all His people and gave them all an inheritance and the reign and the kehunnah and the Miqdash,
2.18: as He promised in the Torah, will shortly show favor upon us, and gather us together out of every land under the shamayim to the qodesh place; for He has delivered us out of great troubles and has qadosh the place.
2.19: Now concerning Yahuḏah Maqqaḇah and his brothers and the purification of the great Hĕyḵal and the dedication of the altar,
2.20: and the battles against Antioḵos Epiphanĕs and Eupator his son,
2.21: and the visible signs that came from the shamayim to those that acted bravely in their honor for the Yahuḏim so that, being but a few, they overcame the whole country, and chased a multitude of foreigners,
2.22: and again recovered the Hĕyḵal renowned all the world over, and freed the city, and upheld the Laws which were declining, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 showing favor to them with all kindness.
2.23: All these things I say, being declared by Yason of Kurĕnĕ in five books, we will attempt to shorten in one volume.
2.24: For considering the limitless number and the difficulty which they find who desire to look into the narrations of the story, for the variety of the matter,
2.25: we have been careful that those who read may have delight, and that those who are eager to commit to memory might have ease, and that all into whose hands it comes might benefit.
2.26: Therefore to we who have taken upon ourselves this painful labor of abridging, it was not easy, but a matter of sweat and watchfulness.
2.27: Even as it is not easy for he that prepares a banquet and seeks the benefit of others, yet for the pleasure of many we will gladly undertake this with great pains,
2.28: leaving to the author the exact handling of every particular, and laboring to follow the rules of an abridgement.
2.29: For as the master builder of a new house must care for the whole building; but he that undertakes to lay it out and paint it, must seek out proper adornments for it; even so I think it is with us.
2.30: To stand upon every point and go over matters at large and to be watchful in particulars, belongs to the first author of the story,
2.31: but to use brevity, and avoid much laboring of the work, is allowed to him that will make an abridgment.
2.32: Here then we will begin the story, only adding this much to that which has been said, that it is a foolish thing to make a long prologue, and to be short in the story itself...

3.1: Now when the qodesh city was inhabited with all peace and the Laws were guarded very well, because of the righteousness of Onyah the kohĕn ha’gadol and his hatred of wickedness,
3.2: it came to be that even the melaḵim themselves honored the place and extolled the Hĕyḵal with their best gifts,
3.3: so that Seleukus of Asia bore all the costs pertaining to the service of the offerings from his own revenues.
3.4: But a certain Shim’on of the tribe of Binyamin, who was made governor of the Hĕyḵal, fell out with the kohĕn ha’gadol about disorder in the city.
3.5: And when he could not overcome Onyah, he went to Apollonios the son of Thraseas, who then was governor of Koĕlĕ Suria and Phoinikĕ,
3.6: and told him that the treasury in Yerushalayim was full of an endless amount of silver, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not pertain to the account of the offerings, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the meleḵ’s hand.
3.7: Now when Apollonios came to the meleḵ, and had showed him some of the silver of which he was told, the meleḵ chose out Heliodorus his treasurer, and sent him with a command to bring him the silver spoken of.
3.8: So Heliodorus promptly took his journey, under pretense of visiting the cities of Koĕlĕ Suria and Phoinikĕ, but indeed to fill the meleḵ’s purpose.
3.9: And when he came to Yerushalayim, and had been received in friendship by the kohĕn ha’gadol of the city, he told him what information was given regarding the silver and declared why he came and asked if these things were indeed so.
3.10: Then the kohĕn ha’gadol told him that there was such silver laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children,
3.11: and that some of it belonged to Hurkanos son of Toḇiyah, a man of high position, and not as that wicked Shim’on had misinformed; the sum of which in total was four hundred talanton of silver and two hundred of gold,
3.12: and that it was altogether impossible that such wrongs should be done to those that had committed it to the qodeshah of the place, and to the esteem and undefiled qodeshah of the Hĕyḵal honored all over the world.
3.13: But because of the meleḵ’s command given him, Heliodorus said that by any means it must be brought into the meleḵ’s treasury.
3.14: So on the day which he appointed, he entered in to order this matter, therefore there was no small distress throughout the whole city.
3.15: But the kohenim, bowing themselves before the altar in their kehunnah garments, called to the shamayim on He that made a Torah concerning matters given to be kept, that they should safely be preserved for such as had committed them to be kept.
3.16: Then whoever the kohĕn ha’gadol had looked in the face, it would have wounded his heart, for his appearance and his change in color made clear the inward agony of his mind.
3.17: For the man was so encompassed with fear and horror of the body, that it was made clear to those that looked upon him what sorrow he now had in his heart.
3.18: Others ran out of their houses gathering to the general supplication, because the place was likely to come into contempt.
3.19: And the women, girded with sackcloth under their breasts, overflowed in the streets, and the maidens that were kept in ran, some to the gates and some to the walls, and others looked out of the windows.
3.20: And all, holding their hands toward the shamayim, made supplication.
3.21: Then it would have pitied a man to see the falling down of the multitude of all sorts, and the fear of the kohĕn ha’gadol being in such an agony.
3.22: They then called upon 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty to guard the matters entrusted safe and secure for those that had committed them.
3.23: Nevertheless Heliodorus executed that which was decreed.
3.24: Now as he was there present with his guard around the treasury, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 of Ruaḥoth and the Prince of all power, caused a great appearance, so that all that though to come in with him were astonished at the power of Elohim and fainted and were greatly frightened.
3.25: For there appeared to them a horse with a fearsome rider upon it, and adorned with a very attractive covering. And it ran fiercely and smote at Heliodorus with its forelegs and it seemed that he that sat upon the horse had a harness completely of gold.
3.26: And two other young men appeared before him, notable in strength, excellent in beauty and splendid in apparel, who stood by him on either side and flogged him continually and gave him very many stripes.
3.27: And Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground and was surrounded with great darkness, but those that were with him picked him up and put him into a palanquin.
3.28: So he, that recently came with a great procession and with all his guard into the treasury, they carried out, being unable to help himself with his weapons, and making it clear they acknowledged the power of Elohim.
3.29: For he, by the hand of Elohim was thrown down, and lay speechless without any expectancy of life.
3.30: And they baraḵ 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 who had miraculously honored His own place, for the Hĕyḵal - which shortly before was full of fear and trouble - when 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty appeared, was filled with joy and gladness.
3.31: Then immediately some friends of Heliodorus who lay ready to breathe his last, pleaded with Onyah that he would call upon the Most High to grant him his life.
3.32: So the kohĕn ha’gadol, suspecting lest the meleḵ should wrongly think that some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by the Yahuḏim, offered an offering for the health of the man.
3.33: Now as the kohĕn ha’gadol was making an atonement, the same young men in the same garments appeared and stood beside Heliodorus saying, “Give Onyah the kohĕn ha’gadol great thanks, because for his sake 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 has granted you life.
3.34: “And seeing that you have been flogged from the shamayim, declare to all men the mighty power of Elohim.” And when they had spoken these words, they no longer appeared.
3.35: So after he had brought an offering to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and made great vows to Him that had saved his life, and embraced Onyah, Heliodorus returned with his army to the meleḵ.
3.36: Then he witnessed to all men the works of the great Elohim, which he had seen with his eyes.
3.37: And when the Meleḵ Heliodorus, who might be a suitable man to be sent yet once again to Yerushalayim said,
3.38: “If you have any enemy or traitor, send him there, and you shall receive him well flogged, if he escapes with his life. For in that place, no doubt; there is a special power of Elohim.
3.39: “For he that dwells in the shamayim has His eye on that place, and defends it; and He beats and destroys those that come to damage it.”
3.40: And the matters concerning Heliodorus and the keeping of the treasury, fell out on this sort.

4.1: This Shim’on now, of whom we spoke before, having been a betrayer of the silver and of his country, slandered Onyah as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils.
4.2: Thus he was bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved good from the city and shown concern for his own nation and was so ardent for the Laws.
4.3: But when their hatred went so far that murders were committed by one of Shim’on’s faction,
4.4: Onyah seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonios - being the governor of Koĕlĕ Suria and Phoinikĕ - raged and increased Shim’on’s evil.
4.5: He went to the meleḵ, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both public and private.
4.6: For he saw that it was impossible that the situation should remain calm, and Shim’on leave his folly, unless the meleḵ looked into it.
4.7: But after the death of Seleukus, when Antioḵos called Epiphanĕs took the reign, Yason the brother of Onyah acted corruptly to be kohĕn ha’gadol,
4.8: promising to the meleḵ by intercession three hundred and sixty talanton of silver, and eighty talanton from another revenue.
4.9: Besides this, he promised to assign a hundred and fifty more if he might have authority to establish a place for exercise, and for the training up of youth in the manner of the gentiles, and to describe those of Yerushalayim by the name of Antioḵeians;
4.10: which when the meleḵ had granted, and he had acquired the rulership into his hand, he promptly brought his own nation to Yawanite manner.
4.11: And he took away the royal privileges granted by special favor to the Yahuḏim by means of Yoḥanan the father of Eupolemus - who went ambassador to Rome for peace and assistance - and putting down the governments which were according to the Torah, he brought up new customs against the Torah.
4.12: For he gladly built an exercise arena under the tower itself, and brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat.
4.13: Now such was the height of Yawanite ways and increase of gentile manners through the exceeding profaneness of Yason, that wicked wretch, and no kohĕn ha’gadol;
4.14: that the kohenim had no heart to serve any more at the altar, but despising the Hĕyḵal and neglecting the slaughterings, hastened to be partakers of the unlawful allowance in the exercise arena, called out after striking the gong;
4.15: not remaining in the honors of their fathers, but loving the esteem of the Yawanites above all.
4.16: For this reason severe calamity came upon them, for those whose custom they followed so earnestly and to whom they desired to be like in every way, came to be their enemies and avengers.
4.17: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the Laws of Elohim, but the time following shall make known these things.
4.18: Now when the meleḵ was present at the quadrennial games that were held at Tsor,
4.19: this shameful Yason sent special messengers from Yerushalayim, who were Antioḵeians to carry three hundred draḵmas of silver to the offering of Heraklĕs, which even the bearers thought not fit to present upon the offering, because it was not right, but to be reserved for other charges.
4.20: This silver then, in regard to the sender, was appointed to Heraklĕs’ offering; but because of the bearers, it was applied to the making of galleys.
4.21: Now when Apollonios the son of Mĕnĕstheos was sent to Mitsrayim for the coronation of Meleḵ Ptolemaeus Philometor, Antioḵos, understanding him not to be well inclined to his affairs, provided for his own safety. So he came to Yapho, and from there to Yerushalayim,
4.22: where he was honorably received by Yason and by the city, and was brought in with torch alight and with great shouting, and so afterward went with his army to Phoinikĕ.
4.23: Three years afterward Yason sent Menelaos, the brother of the same Shim’on, to take the silver to the meleḵ, and to put him in mind of some necessary matters.
4.24: But he, being brought to the presence of the meleḵ, when he had exalted him for the splendid appearance of his power, obtained the kehunnah for himself, offering more than Yason by three hundred talanton of silver.
4.25: So he came with the meleḵ’s authority, bringing nothing worthy of the high kehunnah, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.
4.26: Then Yason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee to the land of the Ammonites;
4.27: so Menelaos gained the principality. But as for the silver that he had promised to the meleḵ, he gave no good order for it, although Sostratos the ruler of the fortress required it,
4.28: for the gathering of the customs belonged to him. Therefore they were both called before the meleḵ.
4.29: Now Menelaos left his brother Lusimaḵos in his place in the kehunnah, and Sostratos left Krĕtĕs, who was governor of the Kuprians.
4.30: While those matters were taking place, those of Tarsos and Mallos revolted because they were given to the meleḵ’s concubine called Antioḵos.
4.31: Then the meleḵ came in haste to appease matters, leaving Andronikos, a man in authority as his deputy.
4.32: Now Menelaos, supposing that he had gained a convenient time, stole some vessels of gold out of the Hĕyḵal, and gave some of them to Andronikos, and some he sold to Tsor and the cities round about.
4.33: When Onyah knew for certain, he reproved him and withdrew himself to a refuge at Daphnĕ, that is near Antioḵeia.
4.34: Therefore Menelaos, taking Andronikos aside, asked him to take Onyah into his hands; who being persuaded and coming to Onyah in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths. And though he was suspected by him, yet he persuaded him to come out from the refuge, whom he promptly shut up without regard for righteousness.
4.35: For which cause, not only the Yahuḏim, but also many of other nations were greatly enraged and were very grieved for the unrighteous murder of the man.
4.36: And when the meleḵ had come again from the places around Kilikia, the Yahuḏim that were in the city and some of the Yawanites that loathed the fact also, complained because Onyah was slain without cause.
4.37: Therefore Antioḵos was deeply sorry and moved to pity, and wept because of the sober and modest behavior of he that was dead.
4.38: And being kindled with wrath, he promptly took away from Andronikos his purple, and tore off his garments, and leading him through the whole city to that very place where he had committed unrighteousness against Onyah, there he slew the cursed murderer. Thus 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 repaid him his punishment as he had deserved.
4.39: Now when many temple robberies had been committed in the city by Lusimaḵos with the consent of Menelaos, and the fruit of which was spread abroad, many vessels of gold already having been carried away, the multitude gathered themselves together against Lusimaḵos.
4.40: So when the common people rose up being filled with rage, Lusimaḵos armed about three thousand men and first began to do violence; a certain Auranus being the leader, a man far gone in years, and no less in folly.
4.41: Some of them then seeing the attempt of Lusimaḵos took stones, some clubs, others taking handfuls of dust that was at hand, threw them all together at Lusimaḵos, and those that attacked them.
4.42: Thus they wounded many of them, and some they struck to the ground, and they forced all of them to flee. But as for the temple-robber himself, they killed him beside the treasury.
4.43: Therefore because of these matters there was an accusation laid against Menelaos.
4.44: Now when the meleḵ came to Tsor, three men that were sent from the senate pleaded the case before him,
4.45: but Menelaos, being now convicted, promised Ptolemaeus the son of Dorumĕnĕs to give him much silver, if he would pacify the meleḵ toward him.
4.46: So Ptolemaeus taking the meleḵ aside into a certain gallery, as it were to get some air, caused him to think differently,
4.47: so that he discharged Menelaos from the accusations, who was causing all the evil however, and those poor men, who, if they had stated their case - even before the Skuthians, should have been judged innocent - those he condemned to death.
4.48: So those that pursued the matter for the city and for the people and for the qodesh vessels, quickly suffered unrighteous punishment.
4.49: Therefore even those of Tsor, moved with hatred for that wicked deed, had them buried honorably.
4.50: And so through the covetousness of those that were of power, Menelaos still remained in authority, increasing in evil, and being a great traitor to the citizens.

5.1: About the same time Antioḵos prepared his second voyage to Mitsrayim.
5.2: And then it came to be, that through all the city for almost forty days, there was seen horsemen running in the air in golden garments, and armed with lances like a band of soldiers,
5.3: and bands of horsemen in array attacking and charging against one another with shaking shields and multitudes of spears and drawing swords and shooting arrows and glittering golden ornaments with harnesses of all kinds.
5.4: Therefore every man prayed that the apparition might turn to good.
5.5: Now when a false rumor had gone out, as though Antioḵos had been dead, Yason took at the least one thousand men, and made a sudden assault on the city; and those that were on the walls retreated, and with the city being eventually taken, Menelaos fled into the fortress.
5.6: But Yason slew his own citizens without pity, not considering that to win the day from them over his own nation would be a very grievous day for him; but thinking they had been his enemies whom he conquered, and not his countrymen.
5.7: However for all this he did not obtain the principality, but in the end received shame for the recompense of his treason, and fled again into the land of the Ammonites.
5.8: In the end therefore, he had an unpleasant return, being accused before Aretas the meleḵ of the Araḇians, fleeing from city to city, pursued by all men, hated as a forsaker of the Laws, and being held in abomination as an open enemy of his country and countrymen, he was thrown out into Mitsrayim.
5.9: So he that had driven many out of their land perished in a strange land, retiring to the Lakedaemonians, and thinking to find support there by reason of his relatives.
5.10: And he that had thrown out many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor any solemn funerals at all, nor tomb with his fathers.
5.11: Now when this that was done came to the meleḵ’s ear, he thought that Yahuḏah had revolted, so departing from Mitsrayim in a rage, he took the city by force of arms,
5.12: and commanded his men of battle not to spare any they met, but to slay any who went up on the houses.
5.13: Thus there was slaughter of young and old; doing away with men, women and children; slaying of maidens and infants.
5.14: And there were eighty thousand destroyed within the space of three whole days, of which forty thousand were slain in the battle, and no fewer sold than slain.
5.15: Yet was he not content with this, but presumed to go into the most qodesh Hĕyḵal of all the world - Menelaos being his guide - that traitor to the Laws and to his own country.
5.16: And taking the qodesh vessels with polluted hands, and with profane hands pulling down those that were dedicated by other melaḵim to the adornment and esteem and honor of the place, he gave away.
5.17: And Antioḵos was so proud of heart that he did not consider that 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 was wroth for a while for the sins of those that dwelt in the city, and therefore his eye was not on the place.
5.18: For had they not been previously entwined in many sins, this man as soon as he had come, had promptly been scourged and put back from his presumption, as Heliodorus was, whom Seleukus the meleḵ sent to view the treasury.
5.19: Nevertheless Elohim did not choose the people for the sake of the place, but the place for the sake of the people.
5.20: And therefore the place itself, that shared with those in the distress that befell the nation, afterward shared in the benefits sent from 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and as it was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty, so again, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty having restored it to favor, was put up with all esteem.
5.21: So when Antioḵos had carried out of the Hĕyḵal one thousand eight hundred talanton, he departed in haste to Antioḵeia, thinking in his pride to sail on the land and pass over the sea on foot, such was the pride of his heart.
5.22: And he left governors to oppress the nation: at Yerushalayim, Philippos, a Phrugian of his land, and in many ways more barbarous than he that appointed him there.
5.23: And at Gerizim: Andronikos, and also Menelaos, who worse than all the rest bore a heavy hand over the citizens, having a malicious heart against his race the Yahuḏim.
5.24: He also sent that detestable ringleader Apollonios with an army of twenty-two thousand, commanding him to slay all those in their prime and to sell the women and the younger ones,
5.25: who coming to Yerushalayim and pretending peace, waited till the qodesh day of the Shabbath, when finding the Yahuḏim keeping a qodesh day, he commanded his men to arm themselves.
5.26: And so he slew all those that went to the celebration of the Shabbath, and running through the city with weapons slew great multitudes.
5.27: But Yahuḏah Maqqaḇah with about nine others, withdrew into the wilderness with his army, and lived in the mountains after the manner of beasts, eating plants continually, lest they should be partakers of the pollution.

6.1: Not long after this, the meleḵ sent an old man of Athĕnai to compel the Yahuḏim to depart from the Laws of their fathers and not to live after the Laws of Elohim,
6.2: and to also pollute the Hĕyḵal in Yerushalayim, and to call it the temple of Zeus Olympios; and the one in Gerizim: of Zeus the defender of foreigners, as those that dwelt in the place desired.
6.3: The coming of this trouble was very grievous to the people,
6.4: for the Hĕyḵal was filled with loose behavior and revelry by the gentiles, who played with whores and went aside with women within the borders of the qodesh places, and besides that, brought in objects that were not right.
6.5: The altar was also filled with abominations which the Torah forbids,
6.6: neither was it allowed for a man to guard Shabbath days or ancient feasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Yahuḏi.
6.7: And every month in the day of the meleḵ’s birth they were taken under bitter constraint to eat of the offerings; and when the fast of Dionusos was kept, the Yahuḏim were compelled to go in the procession of Dionusos carrying ivy.
6.8: And a decree went out to the neighboring cities of the gentiles by the word of Ptolemaeus, against the Yahuḏim, that they should observe the same practice and be partakers of their offerings,
6.9: and whoever would not conform themselves to the ways of the gentiles should be put to death. Then one could see the present misery;
6.10: for there were two women brought who had circumcised their children, whom when they had openly led round about the city - the infants hanging at their breasts - they threw them down from the wall.
6.11: And others that had run together into caves nearby to guard the Shabbath day secretly, being discovered by Philippos, were all burned together, for they would not for conscience defend themselves in honor of the most qodesh day.
6.12: Now I plead to those that read this book, that they do not be discouraged because of these calamities, but that they consider these punishments not to be for destruction, but for a disciplining of our nation.
6.13: For it is a sign of His great goodness, when evil-doers are not given any length of time, but promptly punished.
6.14: For He does not deal with us as with other nations whom 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 patiently awaits to punish, till they have come to the fulness of their sins,
6.15: lest having come to the height of sin, He should take vengeance on us afterwards,
6.16: and therefore He never withdraws His kindness from us. And though He punishes with adversity, yet He never forsakes His people.
6.17: But let this that we have spoken be for a warning to us; and now will we come to the declaring of the matter in a few words.
6.18: Eli’ezer, one of the principal scribes, an aged man and of a well-favored presence, was forced to open his mouth, and to eat pig’s flesh.
6.19: But he, choosing rather to die with honor than to live stained with such an abomination, spat it out, and went to the torture of his own accord,
6.20: as is necessary for those to go that stand firm against such matters that are not Lawful to be tasted even for love of life.
6.21: But those who were in charge of that wicked feast, took aside the man because of the old acquaintance they had with him, and urged him to bring flesh of his own provision, such as was Lawful for him to use, and make as if he ate of the flesh taken from the offering commanded by the meleḵ;
6.22: that in doing so he might be delivered from death, and find favor with them for the old friendship.
6.23: But he began to consider wisely, as was befit for his years and the excellency of his old age and the honor of his head on which grey had come, and his most upright Torah from childhood, or rather the qodesh Torah made and given by Elohim. Therefore he answered accordingly, and requested they immediately send him to the grave.
6.24: “For it is not proper for our age,” he said, “in any way to pretend, whereby many young ones might think that Eli’ezer, being ninety years old, had now gone to a strange religion.
6.25: “And so they, through my hypocrisy and desire to live a little time and a moment longer should be deceived by me and I bring a stain on my old age and make it abominable.
6.26: “For though for the present time I should be delivered from the punishment of men, yet I would not escape the hand of the Almighty, neither alive, nor dead.
6.27: “Therefore now, bravely exchanging this life, I will show myself such a one as befits my age,
6.28: and leave a notable example to those who are young; to die willingly and courageously for the esteemed and qodesh Laws.” And when he had said these words, he immediately went to the torture,
6.29: those leading him changing the kindness they bore him a little before into hatred, because they supposed the previous words came from a desperate being.
6.30: And when he was ready to die with stripes, he groaned and said, “It is known to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 who has the qodesh wisdom, that whereas I might have been delivered from death, I now endure severe pains in body by being beaten, but in spirit I am well content to suffer these, because I revere Him!”
6.31: And so the man died, leaving his death as an example of a noble courage, and a remembrance of strength, not only to young men, but to all his nation.

7.1: It also came to be, that seven brothers with their mother were taken, and compelled by the meleḵ - against the Torah - to eat pig’s flesh, and were tortured with scourges and whips.
7.2: But one of them that spoke first said, “What would you ask or learn from us? We are ready to die, rather than to transgress the Laws of our fathers.”
7.3: Then the meleḵ becoming enraged, commanded pots and cauldrons to be heated.
7.4: These promptly being heated, he commanded to cut out the tongue of he that spoke first, and to cut off the outer parts of his body with the rest of his brothers and his mother looking on.
7.5: Now when he was mutilated in this way over his entire body, he commanded him while still alive to be brought to the fire, and to be fried in the cauldron. And as the smoke of the cauldron spread widely, they encouraged one another with their mother to die bravely saying,
7.6: “𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 Elohim watches over us and in truth has compassion on us, as Mosheh spoke in his song which witnessed to their faces saying, ‘And He has compassion on his servants.’ ”
7.7: So when the first had died in this manner, they brought the second to make him a mockery. And when they had pulled off the skin from his head with the hair, they asked him, “Will you eat before you are tortured over every part of your body?”
7.8: But he answered in his own language and said, “No.” Therefore he also received the next torture in turn as the former had.
7.9: And when he was at the last gasp he said, “In wrath you remove us from this present life, but the Meleḵ of the world shall raise up we who have died for His Laws, unto everlasting ḥai!”
7.10: After him, the third was made a mockery, and when demanded, he immediately put out his tongue and held out his hands bravely
7.11: and said courageously, “These I had from the shamayim and for His Laws I despise them, and from Him I expect to receive them again.”
7.12: Therefore the meleḵ, and those that were with him, marveled at the young man’s courage that he regarded the pains as nothing.
7.13: Now when this man was also dead, they tortured and mutilated the fourth in a similar way.
7.14: So when he was ready to die he said, “It is good to be put to death by men; to look for expectancy from Elohim to be raised up again by Him. As for you, you shall have no resurrection to ḥai.”
7.15: Afterward they brought the fifth also, and mutilated him.
7.16: Then he looked at the meleḵ and said, “You have power over men, you are corruptible, you do what you want; yet do not think that our nation is forsaken by Elohim.
7.17: “But wait a while and see His great power, how He will distress you and your seed.”
7.18: After him they also brought the sixth, who being ready to die said, “Do not be deceived by any means, for we suffer these matters because of ourselves, having sinned against our Elohim; therefore great matters are done to us.
7.19: “But do not think, you who takes in hand to strive against Elohim, that you shall escape unpunished.”
7.20: But the mother was greater above all and worthy of honorable remembrance; for when she saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day, she bore it with good courage because of the expectancy that she had in 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
7.21: She also encouraged every one of them in her own language. Filled with a courageous spirit and stirring up her womanly thoughts with a brave face, she said to them,
7.22: “I cannot tell how you came into my womb; for I neither gave you breath nor life, nor was it I that formed the members of every one of you.
7.23: “But without doubt the Creator of the world who formed the generation of man and revealed the beginning of all, will also give you of His own kindness, breath and ḥai again, as you disregard now your own beings for the sake of His Laws.”
7.24: Now while the youngest was still alive, Antioḵos, thinking himself despised and suspecting it to be a reproachful speech, did not only encourage him with words, but also assured him with oaths, that he would make him both a rich and fortunate man if he would turn from the Laws of his fathers, and that he would also accept him as his friend, and trust him with affairs.
7.25: But when the young man would in no way listen to him, the meleḵ called his mother and encouraged her that she should counsel the young man to save his life.
7.26: And when he had encouraged her with many words, she promised him that she would counsel her son.
7.27: But she, bowing herself toward him, laughing the cruel tyrant to scorn, spoke in her nation’s language in this way; “O my son, have pity on me who bore you nine months in my womb, and gave you three years and nourished you and brought you up to this age and endured the troubles of teaching.
7.28: “Please my son, look on the shamayim and the earth and all that is in them and consider that Elohim made them from that which was not; and so was mankind made likewise.
7.29: “Do not fear this torturer, but being worthy of your brothers, accept your death that I may receive you again in kindness with your brothers.”
7.30: While she was still speaking these words, the young man said, “Whom do you wait for? I will not obey the meleḵ’s command, but I will obey the Command of the Torah that was given to our fathers by Mosheh.
7.31: “And you, who has been the author of all evil against the Iḇrim, shall not escape the hands of Elohim!
7.32: “For we suffer because of our sins,
7.33: and although the living Elohim is wroth with us a little while for our discipline and correction, yet He shall be at one again with his servants.
7.34: “But you, O wicked man, and of all others most evil, do not be lifted up without a cause nor puffed up with uncertain expectancies, lifting up your hand against the servants of Elohim;
7.35: for you have not yet escaped the judgment of Ĕl Shaddai, who sees all.
